Orthopaedic injuries often are associated with soft-tissue trauma. Successful fracture
fixation requires adequate soft-tissue coverage to minimize the risk of infection,
promote fracture healing, and restore form and function. Skin grafts and flaps are the
most commonly used techniques for tissue reconstruction.
Grafts
A graft does not have a blood supply.
The three main phases of nutrition for graft survival are imbibition, inosculation, and
angiogenesis.

Grafts
A graft is any piece of tissue that is harvested from one part of the body without a blood
supply and then transferred to another anatomic location. The recipient site supplies the
necessary nutrients for the graft to survive through a series of well-defined stages.
Imbibition (ie, passive flow of nutrients and growth factors from the recipient bed),
inosculation (ie, blood vessels in the graft grow to meet vessels in the recipient bed), and
angiogenesis (ie, new vessels form between the graft and recipient tissues) are the three
main phases of nutrition for graft survival. Grafts can include any type of tissue,
including skin, bone, and cartilage.1
Grafts require a vascularized recipient site for survival. Acceptable recipient sites include
granulating wounds, muscle, and tendon or bone if the paratenon or periosteum is
intact. A graft will not survive if the recipient site does not have an adequate blood
supply. Therefore, denuded bone, which frequently is present after open fractures,
requires an alternative type of reconstruction.2
Skin grafts are the most common type of graft. Using a dermatome for a split-thickness
skin graft or a knife for a full-thickness skin graft, the surgeon can harvest skin from any
part of the body and transfer it to another. Split-thickness skin grafts have the benefit of
being easily harvested and expandable to cover large defects and have a high likelihood

of successful adherence; however, split-thickness skin grafts are thin, prone to shearing,
and are not ideal for areas exposed to external pressures (eg, shoes, gloves). Split-
thickness skin grafts also result in high rates of contracture and are not ideal for mobile
surfaces, such as joints. Full-thickness skin grafts result in lower rates of contracture and
decreased donor site morbidity because the donor site often can be closed primarily
rather than left as a large raw surface, which is observed with a split-thickness skin graft;
However, full-thickness skin grafts result in lower rates of adherence, require longer
surgical times, and cannot be used for large areas.3
Flaps
A flap name is based on its components.
A flap has an intact blood supply, and its blood supply can be random, axial, and pedicled or
free.
A free flap is harvested with an intact artery and vein to supply the tissue.

Flaps
A flap is defined as any piece of tissue that can be harvested from one part of the body
with an intact blood supply and then transferred to another part. The flap can consist of
skin, fascia, muscle, bone, nerve, blood vessels, or any combination of tissues. The flap
name is based on its components. For example, an adipofascial flap contains only fat
and fascia. Similarly, an osteocutaneous flap contains bone and skin.
The blood supply of a flap can be random, axial, and pedicled or free. In a random
pattern flap, the blood supply to the tissue is unnamed. In general, for a random pattern
flap, the width of the flap should have a 1:1 ratio to the length of the flap to maximize
viability. Elevation of the surrounding skin with advancement to cover an open wound is
an example of a random pattern flap. An axial flap is a piece of tissue in which the
pedicle incorporates a named artery or vein. The pedicle refers to the tissue containing
the blood supply to the flap. A common axial flap is the groin flap, which can be used to
cover soft-tissue injuries of the hand or wrist. The named blood vessel supplying the

groin flap is the superficial circumflex iliac artery. Pedicled flaps are axial flaps that are
rotated or transposed from one area to another without disrupting the blood supply.
One of the most common pedicled flaps is the gastrocnemius flap, which is used to cover
soft-tissue defects of the proximal one-third of the tibia. Finally, a free flap is any piece of
tissue that is harvested by transecting the pedicle containing the intact artery and vein
that supply the tissue from its origination. After a free flap is dissected, it can be
transferred to any part of the body given a recipient artery and vein are present. The
artery and vein of the flap are then connected to the recipient artery and vein using a
microscope.4
Flap delay is a method commonly used to increase the vascularity of a flap before
transfer. During a flap delay, all secondary blood supplies to the flap are sacrificed, and
the flap is isolated on the single desired artery and vein. If a flap is delayed, choke
vessels within the flap that normally are closed become patent, leading to increased
vascularity of the flap, which may improve the likelihood of flap survival. After the
surgeon performs the initial flap delay procedure, 1 to 3 weeks are allowed to pass so
the flap can acclimate to its new blood supply before it is transferred to a new anatomic
location.5
Tissue expansion is another type of flap reconstruction in which a flap is created by
placing expandable balloons in the subcutaneous space.4 Over the course of several
weeks, the balloons are expanded using saline to create excess skin and subcutaneous
tissue that can be used as a flap to cover a defect. Although reconstructive surgeons
commonly use tissue expansion for various defects, such as for breast reconstruction,
tissue expansion is a slow process and often is not a first-line reconstructive option for
traumatic injuries that require more timely coverage.6
The Reconstructive Ladder
If a vascularized wound is present, then a graft can be used.
If a nonvascularized wound is present, then a flap must be used.
If a white structure (ie, cartilage, tendon without paratenon, and/or bone without periosteum)
is present, then a flap is needed.

Replace like with like regarding the type of tissue missing and the type of tissue needed.
For defects of the proximal third of the tibia, the gastrocnemius muscle flap often is preferred.
For defects of the middle third of the tibia, a soleus muscle flap can be used if it has not been
damaged by the injury.
For defects of the distal third of the tibia and foot, a free flap is commonly preferred.

The Reconstructive Ladder
The reconstructive ladder is the name of the paradigm that reconstructive surgeons use
in deciding between various reconstructive options7 (Figure 1). The surgeon should aim
to start with the simplest method available and work his or her way up the ladder until
the appropriate option is selected. By adhering to the reconstructive ladder, the surgeon
ensures that the most direct method for reconstruction is attempted first, thereby
preserving more advanced or complicated methods for an unpredicted event, such as
failed reconstruction or recurrence of the wound.
Figure 1 Image shows the soft-tissue reconstructive ladder. (Reproduced with
permission from Janis JE, Kwon RK, Attinger CE: The new reconstructive ladder:
Modifications to the traditional model. Plast Reconstr Surg 2011;127[suppl 1]:205S-212S.)

The bottom rungs of the ladder—the simplest reconstruction options that do not
necessitate a graft for healing—are primary and secondary intention. Primary intention
is direct dermal healing from opposed wound edges that results in minimal scarring and
contracture. Secondary intention results from unopposed wound edges, and healing
occurs from the base of the wound, resulting in more scarring and wound contracture.
In evaluating a wound, the surgeon must assess the vascularity of the tissues, degree of
contamination or amount of soft-tissue necrosis, size of the wound, time needed to
coverage, and presence or absence of white structures. White structures include
denuded cartilage, tendon without paratenon, and bone without periosteum. For simple
wounds with adequate soft tissue for direct closure, such as a laceration, the wound
edges can be repaired after thorough irrigation and débridement. If adequate soft tissue
is not available for direct closure or if considerable contamination is present, the
reconstructive surgeon may elect to allow the wound to heal via secondary intention or
may elect to close the wound after multiple débridement procedures (ie, delayed
primary closure or tertiary intention); however, secondary intention usually is reserved
for wounds with exposed vital structures and no urgency for reconstruction. Primary,
secondary, and tertiary intention all require the presence of adequate vascularized and
healthy tissue to allow for wound healing.
Injuries with extensive soft-tissue loss or exposed vital structures often require a flap or
graft. In addition, flaps and grafts are necessary if the timing of coverage is critical. For
example, soft-tissue coverage of exposed bone or hardware should be performed within
the first few days of injury to minimize the risk of infection (ie, osteomyelitis) and/or
hardware contamination. With these injuries, healing via secondary intention is
contraindicated, and, often, inadequate soft tissue is available for reconstruction via
primary or tertiary intention.
Moving up the ladder for severe injuries requires a graft or flap. The decision between a
graft or flap depends on the status of the blood supply at the recipient site. If a
vascularized wound is present, then a graft can be used; otherwise, a flap will be
necessary. The presence of white structures often indicates that a flap is necessary. In
addition, cavitary lesions (ie, multiple layer defects) require flap reconstruction to fill the
defect and minimize the risk of fluid accumulation (ie, seroma or hematoma) and

infection. In general, open fractures should be reconstructed within 7 days to minimize
the risk of infection; however, the timing of reconstruction depends on multiple factors,
including the patient’s overall health, medical optimization, decontamination of the
wound bed, and the plan for fracture fixation.1
Another important guiding principle for reconstruction is to replace like with like. In
other words, if the defect is missing only skin and subcutaneous tissue, then a
fasciocutaneous flap should be selected. If muscle and skin are missing, then a
musculocutaneous flap would be the most appropriate option.8
Defects of the Upper Extremity

Defects of the Upper Extremity
Restoring form and function to the upper extremity is a challenge given the complexity
of hand, wrist, elbow, and shoulder range of motion. The method necessary for
reconstruction typically depends on the location of the injury.
For open fractures of the hand, various local flap options involving skin and
subcutaneous tissue have been described. For defects of the volar thumb, the Moberg
flap, which isolates the volar skin on the bilateral digital neurovascular pedicles, has
been well described (Figure 2). For defects of the dorsal thumb, the first dorsal
metacarpal artery flap commonly is used.9
Open injuries of the hand and wrist often can be reconstructed with the use of a radial
forearm flap, which is an axial flap of skin and subcutaneous tissue based on the radial
artery and cephalic vein. During this procedure, the proximal radial artery and the
cephalic vein are transected, and the pedicle to the flap is via the distal artery and vein,
with blood supplied from the ulnar vessels through an intact palmar arch. An Allen test
should be performed before elevating a radial forearm flap to ensure an intact palmar
arch.10 The posterior interosseous artery flap also is well described, but typically the

posterior interosseous artery is not as robust as the radial vessels. The pedicled groin
flap or an abdominal-based perforator flap are other popular options.11
Defects of the elbow also can be reconstructed with the use of a radial forearm flap;
however, for proximal arm defects, the distal radial artery and cephalic vein are
transected, and the flap is rotated proximally. The lateral arm flap, based on the
posterior radial collateral artery, also is a popular option12(Figure 3).
Defects of the upper arm and shoulder often are reconstructed with the use of a
latissimus flap. The latissimus flap can be harvested with skin or muscle only. The
latissimus muscle also can be transferred as a neurotized functional flap to restore
elbow flexion, which may be necessary in patients with a brachial plexus injury.13

The foot and ankle are challenging anatomic areas for reconstruction. The skin overlying
this area is thin and pliable. Therefore, injuries to the foot and ankle often involve large
areas of exposed tendon and bone. In addition, the blood supply to this area can be
altered by traumatic injury or baseline vascular disease. Often, vascular studies,
including CT angiography, angiography, ankle brachial indices, and transcutaneous
oxygen pressures, may help guide the reconstructive surgeon to the most appropriate
treatment option (Videos 1 through 6).14

Pedicled flap reconstructions of the foot and ankle are limited. Popular options include
the medial plantar artery flap for plantar foot defects or the sural flap for dorsal foot
defects and distal leg defects. Although the sural flap is a well-described option, it often
must be delayed before successful transfer.15
In general, defects of the distal third of the tibia and foot require free flap reconstruction
(Figure 4). The posterior and anterior tibial vessels are popular recipient vessels;
however, because free flap reconstruction requires sacrificing one of these vessels to
supply the flap, documenting three-vessel runoff to the foot via preoperative imaging
studies is important. In patients in whom the vessels to the distal leg have been
compromised, advanced techniques, such as end-to-side vessel anastomoses or the
creation of an arterial-venous loop, are required. In addition, ensuring that the

Popular free flap options for the foot and distal leg include the gracilis muscle for slender
defects, the latissimus muscle for large defects, and the anterolateral thigh flap (ie, flap
composed of skin and subcutaneous tissue based on the lateral descending branch of
the profunda femoris artery). If a muscle flap is used, it will need to be covered with a
skin graft. The skin graft can be applied at the time of the muscle flap or 2 to 5 days after
flap survival is confirmed. An important consideration before harvesting the latissimus
muscle flap is the likelihood of amputation if reconstruction is unsuccessful. Because
latissimus muscle function is important for successful crutch or walker use, harvesting of
this muscle should be limited if the likelihood of eventual amputation is high.17

Defects of the middle third of the tibia often can be reconstructed using a soleus muscle
flap. The soleus muscle flap is based on segmental perforators and can be harvested by
transecting the proximal or distal end of the muscle. The flap is robust, but donor site
morbidity is more problematic because the soleus is a powerful flexor of the foot.18 If
the soleus muscle has been damaged substantially by the traumatic event, free tissue
transfer may be necessary for soft-tissue coverage of the middle third of the tibia.
For the proximal third of the tibia, the gastrocnemius muscle flap is commonly
preferred. The medial or lateral head of the gastrocnemius can be harvested. If the
lateral gastrocnemius muscle is selected, careful attention must be paid to the plane of
dissection near the fibular head to avoid injury to the peroneal nerve.19
Defects of the thigh are commonly reconstructed using local muscle flaps, such as the
gracilis, rectus, sartorius, and hamstring muscles. The multitude of muscles in the thigh
often provide adequate soft-tissue coverage; however, large defects may have large
spaces that may require drain placement to prevent fluid accumulation. In patients with
severe soft-tissue loss, free flap reconstruction or an abdominally based muscle flap (ie,
rectus muscle) may be necessary.20
